title: 95% Automated Isn't the Same as 95% Correct
description: An automation-rate metric tells you how much work a system handled without a human — it says nothing about whether that work was actually right, and the two get confused constantly.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish an automation-rate metric from an accuracy metric
Design a validation checkpoint that measures correctness independently of throughput

contentSections.body: Three months into an invoice-processing automation, the client reports the system is handling 95% of invoices 'automatically' — a headline ROI number everyone's happy with. Nobody has checked what 'handled automatically' actually means for those invoices: were they processed correctly, or just processed without a human looking at them? You pull a random sample of 50 from the automated 95% and manually check them against the source documents. Four are wrong — a supplier code misread, a quantity error, two duplicate payments that should've been caught. The 95% automation-rate metric never had a mechanism to distinguish 'automated and correct' from 'automated and silently wrong.'

The specific skill here is building in a validation checkpoint — a recurring random sample, manually checked against ground truth — that's independent of the automation rate itself. Automation rate measures throughput: how much work happened without a human touching it. It says nothing about correctness, and a client, and sometimes a consultant, can mistake one for the other because both numbers get reported as 'the AI is working well.'

Real ROI has to be measured on the same axis as the risk it's replacing. Hours saved is only genuine ROI if the manual process that used to catch a 4-in-50 error rate hasn't quietly disappeared along with the automation. A believable ROI claim needs both numbers — the automation rate and an ongoing, sampled accuracy rate — not just the one that looks better in a slide.

contentSections.scenario:
Client's reported metric: 95% of invoices processed automatically, 5% flagged for human review.
Actual finding from a random sample of 50 'automated' invoices: 4 contain real errors (misread supplier code, quantity error, two duplicate payments) that were never caught, because nothing checks the automated 95% for correctness, only whether a human touched it.
contentSections.question: What does the 95% automation-rate metric actually fail to measure?

options.label: Whether the automatically-processed invoices are actually correct, not just unreviewed
How fast the system processes each invoice
How much the system costs to run per invoice

feedback.whether-automated-work-correct: Correct. 95% automated only tells you 95% of invoices went through without a human review step — it has no built-in mechanism to check whether those invoices were processed accurately. The sampled check is what surfaces the 4-in-50 error rate the automation-rate metric was structurally blind to.
feedback.processing-speed: Speed isn't what's being measured or claimed here — the 95% figure is about what fraction of invoices skipped human review, not how quickly any individual invoice was processed.
feedback.operating-cost: Cost isn't the axis this metric or this problem is about. The gap is specifically between 'processed without a human' and 'processed correctly' — a correctness question, not a cost question.

contentSections.concept: An automation-rate metric answers 'how much of this work did the system do without a human,' which is a throughput measure. It does not and structurally cannot answer 'was the work correct,' which requires an independent check against ground truth — a random sample manually verified, run on an ongoing basis, not the automation-rate number itself.

contentSections.body: An automation-rate number answers 'how much work did the system do,' not 'was the work correct.' Real ROI measurement requires an ongoing sampled accuracy check independent of the automation metric itself, or errors can hide inside the number everyone's celebrating.

title: A Number Going Down Isn't Automatically Good News
description: A metric improving after automation can mean the underlying problem actually got better, or it can mean the automation just moved where the problem gets caught — the two look identical from the headline number alone.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when an improved metric might reflect a shifted measurement point rather than genuine improvement
Design a downstream, independent check that distinguishes real improvement from shifted measurement

contentSections.body: A manufacturing client implements AI-powered camera inspection for defect detection and reports a 30% reduction in defective units shipped — a genuinely impressive-sounding result. Before signing off on this as proof the AI improved quality, you ask one question: where does that 30% figure actually come from — customer returns and post-shipment root-cause data, or just the AI inspection system's own defect classifications, with nobody checking those classifications against what customers actually experience?

This is a different failure mode than the previous lesson's automation-rate confusion, but it rhymes: a metric can genuinely improve for a reason that isn't the one being assumed. If "30% fewer defects shipped" is calculated from the AI system's own classifications — units it flagged and pulled for rework or scrap, compared against the old human-inspection rate — the AI is effectively grading its own homework. It can hit that number two very different ways: by catching genuinely more real defects, or by being more aggressive and flagging (and scrapping) units that would actually have been fine, which also reduces what ships as "defective" by the system's own count, just at the cost of discarding good product instead of catching bad product.

Both explanations can produce the identical self-reported 30% figure. They have completely different implications for whether the client should trust the system, expand it, or reduce downstream inspection staff — one is real quality improvement, the other is expensive waste dressed up as a quality metric. Telling them apart requires a check that doesn't come from the AI system's own output — customer returns, or manual root-cause sampling on what the AI actually flagged.

contentSections.scenario: Client's reported result: 30% fewer defective units shipped after deploying AI-powered inspection. That 30% figure is derived entirely from the AI inspection system's own defect classifications — no customer-return data or post-shipment root-cause analysis has been examined.
contentSections.question: What's the specific gap in this measurement that could make '30% fewer defects shipped' misleading?

options.label: A metric derived entirely from the AI system's own classifications can't distinguish 'genuinely fewer real defects' from 'the AI over-flags and scraps more borderline-but-actually-good units' — both lower the self-reported defect count
Camera-based inspection is inherently less reliable than human visual inspection
A 30% reduction is too small a sample to be statistically meaningful

feedback.self-reported-cant-distinguish: Correct. When the improvement metric comes entirely from the AI system's own classifications, the system is effectively grading its own work — it has no way to reveal whether a flagged unit was actually defective or a false positive being scrapped unnecessarily. Both explanations lower the self-reported defect count identically, and only an independent check (customer returns, manual sampling of what got flagged) can tell them apart.
feedback.ai-cameras-unreliable: This isn't the issue being raised — the lesson isn't questioning whether camera-based detection works technically, it's questioning whether a metric the AI system generates about itself can validate its own accuracy, regardless of how reliable the cameras are mechanically.
feedback.thirty-percent-too-small: Sample size isn't the gap here — even a large, statistically solid 30% reduction, if derived entirely from the AI's own classifications, still can't distinguish real improvement from over-flagging. The problem is the metric's source, not how much data backs it.

contentSections.mechanism: A metric that an automated system generates entirely from its own output can improve for reasons that have nothing to do with genuine quality gains — the system catching more real defects is indistinguishable, from the self-reported number alone, from the system scrapping more good units it mistakenly flagged. Validating real improvement requires an independent, downstream check (customer returns, manual root-cause sampling) that doesn't rely on the automated system's own judgment about its own accuracy.

contentSections.body: When an automated system reports an improvement metric derived entirely from its own output, ask what else could produce that same number besides genuine progress — and check somewhere downstream and independent (customer returns, manual sampling) before recommending the client trust or expand the system based on the number it's reporting about itself.
